item.title: Data shows 73% decline in world’s wildlife population – and more animals are not being counted
item.description: The numbers gathered by the Living Planet Index numbers, which are the most comprehensive available, are still far from complete.
item.content:encoded:
Wildlife populations around the world have declined by an average of 73% since 1970. That’s according to the WWF’s new 2026 Living Planet Index – a major estimate, updated every two years, of the changing state of nature. This does not mean that 73% of the world’s animals have disappeared. Rather, it is the average decline in the size of wildlife populations that is being monitored.

The index is one of the metrics used to track progress towards the UN’s biodiversity goals and shapes narratives of biodiversity loss across the world. But the data behind that 73% headline, one of the most comprehensive available, is still far from complete.

Very few, outside of those of us working at the coalface of handling biodiversity data, understand just how poorly wild animal populations are monitored. Though the world faces the joint crises of climate change and biodiversity loss, we can track climate change through thousands of weather stations or measures of atmospheric CO₂. Biodiversity is far harder to measure. Counting wildlife is highly resource intensive, generally can’t be done from space, and systematic monitoring is extremely patchy.

What this means is that, relative to the data we do possess, there are far, far more wildlife populations...

item.title: US lawmakers urge Trump official to discuss police excesses on protesters during India visit
item.description: They expressed concern about a ‘pattern of repression and wrongful detention’ during demonstrations against the CEC Gyanesh Kumar and the SIR.

Rubio will be visiting Mumbai and Jamnagar between October 19 and October 22. External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar will travel to Mumbai to meet the Trump official on October 20.

In a social media post on Saturday, Indian-born Jayapal said that the US and India have an obligation to defend human rights as the world’s largest democracies.

In a letter addressed to Rubio on Friday, Jayapal, Omar, Jim McGovern, Rashida Tlaib, Eleanor Holmes Norton, and Jesus Garcia expressed concern about a “pattern of repression, wrongful detention, and excessive use of force” by authorities in India during nationwide protests to demand Kumar’s resignation.

item.title: Sally Rooney’s books are being withdrawn from sale in the UK due to her support for Palestine Action
item.description: Her intention to provide financial assistance for the organisation, in the form of donated royalties, may have legal consequences in the UK.
item.content:encoded:
Internationally acclaimed Irish novelist Sally Rooney has announced that she is being forced to withdraw her books from sale in the United Kingdom. This is due to her support for the direct action protest group Palestine Action, which the British government proscribed as a terrorist organisation in June 2025.

Rooney is one of the most visible and exciting literary novelists of the past decade. Her novels have largely focused on nuanced, psychologically acute portrayals of young adult relationships. She uses these often fraught and ambiguous romantic entanglements as a lens for exploring the complexities and cultural anxieties of life in the 21st century.

Her titles typically sell more than 500,000 copies in the UK alone. The BBC adaptation of Normal People, her second novel, has attracted 62.7 million views.

Rooney is based in Ireland, where there is no prohibition on Palestine Action. However, her intention to provide financial assistance for the organisation, in the form of donated royalties, may have legal consequences in the UK. Section 15 of the 2000 Terrorism Act makes it an offence if one “provides money or other property, and knows or has reasonable cause to suspect that it will or may be used for the purposes of terrorism”. Under the Act, this is punishable by a maximum prison sentence of 14 years.

item.title: As Kashmir swaps paddy with apple orchards, food security and water concerns arise
item.description: The shift from could alter the Valley’s groundwater recharge patterns and lead to growing dependence on rice from outside.
item.content:encoded:
“Twenty years ago, all this was paddy,” says Nazir Ahmad, a farmer from Qaimoh, a village in south Kashmir’s Kulgam district, pointing at the rows of apple saplings that now cover his land. Today, much of that landscape has changed. The irrigation channels set up for paddy still exist, running through the fields as they always have. However, the paddy they once fed has given way to apple plantations.

Across Kashmir, farmers are increasingly replacing food crops with horticulture, especially apple orchards, as they seek higher returns amid rising cultivation costs.

For many growers, the calculation is straightforward. Paddy offers modest returns, while apples, particularly high-density plantations, promise significantly higher earnings. The move makes economic sense for individual farmers. However, this is now leading to Kashmir Valley becoming increasingly dependent on outside states for its staple food – rice.

Nisar Ahmed from Kulgam district in Kashmir, used to cultivate paddy on his nine-kanal (0.46 hectares) farmland, which earned him between Rs 30,000 and Rs 50,000 annually. A few years ago, he converted the land into a high-density apple orchard because he was facing losses. item.title: Bailable warrant issued against Dhruv Rathee in 2018 defamation case
item.description: In May 2018, the YouTuber posted a video alleging that the Bharatiya Janata Party’s publicity wing had bribed the complainant to defame him.
item.content:encoded:
A Delhi court on Saturday issued a bailable warrant against YouTuber Dhruv Rathee in a defamation case filed against him in 2018 regarding a video he had posted on his channel, reported Bar and Bench.

The case had been filed by Vikas Sankrityayan, alias Vikas Pandey, after Rathee posted a video in May 2018 alleging that the Bharatiya Janata Party’s publicity wing had bribed the complainant to defame the YouTuber.

Then-Delhi Chief Minister Arvind Kejriwal had shared the video on social media.

On Saturday, Judicial Magistrate Rahul Jain of Saket Court was told that summons could not be served to Rathee earlier this week because his home was found locked, reported Bar and Bench.

On October 12, the court issued summons to Rathee after Pandey moved an application seeking early hearing of the matter on the grounds that the YouTuber, who otherwise lives abroad, was in India for protests against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and the special intensive revision of electoral rolls, reported Live Law.

The next hearing is scheduled for October 31.

On October 10, Rathee was detained by the Delhi Police from Gurugram ahead of a protest by youth groups to demand the resignation of Kumar. The YouTuber had arrived in the national capital a day earlier to participate in the protest.

item.description: A novel featuring cannibals, a civil war in America, a ‘double’ novel about two women, and more.
item.content:encoded:

Exit Party, Emily St John Mandel

2031. America is at war with itself, but for the first time in weeks there is some hope: the Republic of California has been declared, the curfew in Los Angeles is lifted, and everyone in the city is going to a party.

Ari, newly released from prison, arrives with her friend Gloria just as a fragile new era begins. But there are people at the party who shouldn’t be there. Something is very wrong …

Years later, living a different life in Paris, Ari remains haunted by that night. Whatever happened at the party fractured her sense of reality – and may hold the key to a very different world.

item.title: Internet access a fundamental right for all, including children, says SC
item.description: ‘To deny the same altogether would be as absurd as saying children below a certain age do not have a freedom of speech worth expressing,’ said the bench.
item.content:encoded:
The Supreme Court has said that every citizen, including children, has a fundamental right to use the internet.

“To deny the same altogether would be as absurd as saying children below a certain age do not have a conscience worth protecting or a freedom of speech worth expressing,” said a bench of Justices JB Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran in an order passed on Thursday.

The bench was hearing a petition alleging that social media platforms were failing to meet their legal obligations to report child sexual exploitation and abuse material to the authorities.

In its judgement, the court deliberated whether children should be completely shielded from the internet and social media platforms.

However, it pointed out that children's safety and freedom were not at odds. “Our children are entitled to both,” the court noted.

The observations came months after the BBC reported that it had found that social media platform Instagram, which is owned by Meta, had been running paid advertisements that promote child sexual abuse material in India.

Publishing or transmitting child sexual abuse material is illegal and constitutes a serious criminal offence under the 2000 Information Technology Act and the 2012 Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act.

item.title: ‘I wrote a children’s book about an insult I faced. Later, I had the same thought about my daughter’
item.description: Tamil American novelist and essayist Lakshmi Iyer on ‘colourism’.
item.content:encoded:
I typed the word and stopped. Kaali. Two syllables, said by a grandmother to a 12-year-old, in a book meant for readers who are ten. The cursor blinked after the i. Outside, the school bus trundled past our home. I was relieved to get away from my manuscript to make coffee for the kids. Excavating memories is never fun.

Kaali. Black one. Dark one. Is it a slur? Kaali is an adjective, a nickname. It masquerades as concern. It comes from the people who love you, over breakfast, with a palm against your cheek.

‘Even though she is dark, she glows’

I know this because I was that child. Sixth grade, maybe seventh, and Amma is mixing kadalai maavu with paal yedu and a pinch of manjal podi, spreading the creamy paste across my face, waiting for it to dry to a crust before washing it off. I quite enjoyed the ritual, the feeling of amma’s soft palms against my cheek, the chill of the paste evaporating from the heat of my skin, the film tightening the skin until it stretched and you could no longer smile or speak. I used to stand in front of the mirror, my turmeric-tinged face staring back at me like a mask....

item.title: How photography helped physicist Bibha Chowdhuri see the invisible in the 1930s
item.description: The scientist used light-sensitive plates to trace cosmic particles, contributing to pioneering research in particle physics.
item.content:encoded:
In 1939, a 26-year-old physicist published an article that contains what, at first, reads like instructions for an eccentric treasure hunt: place photographic plates in a refrigerator in Calcutta, in Darjeeling or in a Dak Bungalow at Sandakphu. But Bibha Chowdhuri was not looking for buried treasure. She was looking for traces of the invisible.

The plates had been prepared with samarium sulphate and exposed for months to cosmic radiation. When two of those placed at Sandakphu were developed, they revealed 30 “star-like tracks” – microscopic records of nuclear disintegration. The photographs transformed an otherwise invisible encounter between cosmic rays and matter into something that could be seen and studied.

Chowdhuri’s experiment belonged to a new kind of scientific image-making, pioneered in part by physicist Marietta Blau, in which photographic emulsions became detectors of subatomic events. Working with DM Bose at Calcutta’s Bose Institute, Chowdhuri would go on to develop methods for distinguishing particles by the tracks they left in photographic plates. Her work formed part of a chain of experiments that culminated in Cecil Powell’s Nobel Prize-winning research on mesotrons.

Much of what is known about Chowdhuri’s life and work has been compiled by physicists Suprakash C Roy and Rajinder Singh in their biography A Jewel...

item.title: Weekend watch: ‘Tenzing’ brings the first successful Mount Everest expedition home
item.description: Jennifer Peedom’s biopic is out on Apple TV.
item.content:encoded:
Tenzing is very much a biopic of the moment, made in a time of urgent conversations about who gets to tell their own stories and how. Although directed by an Australian, the film is focused on the ascent of the most famous Sherpa to have summited Mount Everest.

In the history books, Tenzing Norgay is hyphenated with the New Zealand mountaineer Edmund Hillary when discussing their feat of becoming the first men to have successfully scaled the world’s highest peak. But in Jennifer Peedom’s Tenzing, Hillary is just one of many people whom Norgay meets over his eventful life.

The film, which is out on Apple TV, stars Tibetan actor Genden Phuntsok as Norgay. Indian actor Tenizin Dhala reunites with his Shambhala co-star Thinley Lhamo to play the younger Norgay and Norgay’s first wife Dawa.

The 125-minute film moves between the present, when Norgay joins a British expedition that includes Edmund Hillary (Tom Hiddleston) in 1953, and Norgay’s experiences as a child and a young adult. Right from a young age, Norgay is desperate to climb the mountain that he worships. The world calls it Mount Everest, after a British surveyor. Norgay knows the mountain as Chomolangma – Mother Goddess of the Earth.

item.title: In pictures: Art and dissent by Bengal’s outspoken Durga Puja pandals in a changed political climate
item.description: Some pandals have embraced overtly religious and nationalist narratives while others have tried to be subversive, though not openly.
item.content:encoded:
Last year, around the time of Durga Puja, public anxiety in West Bengal was mounting with reports of Bengali-speaking people being expelled across the border after being accused of being Bangladeshi.

There was nervousness about citizenship rights and the right to vote due to the approaching Special Intensive Revision of the electoral rolls.

In response, Durga Puja pandals erected for the state’s most popular festival became powerful vehicles for asserting Bengali identity.

For instance, the theme at the Chaltabagan Sarbojanin pandal in Kolkata was “Ami Banglay Bolchi”, I Am Speaking Bengali. It traced the history of the Bengali language. The Aswininagar Bandhumahal pandal explored the historical journeys of Bengalis through changing political and riverine landscapes. The pandal of the Ramgarh Raipur Club told the stories of migrant workers who could not return home for the festival.

These were artistic interventions confronting exclusion in a political climate in which language and identity had become grounds for suspicion.

item.title: ‘How to Date a Fanatic’: Aruni Kashyap’s new novel is hopeful of getting a more tolerant India
item.description: The characters, who mostly belong to the North East and have lived through violence, seem to know better than many how to negotiate a conflict-ridden India.
item.content:encoded:
While reading Aruni Kashyap’s second novel, How to Date a Fanatic, I was confronted with a curious and delicious problem – how does one slot this novel and the novelist? When Kashyap debuted with A House with a Thousand Stories in 2013, a coming-of-age story about young Pablo set against the backdrop of insurgency, the novel could firmly be located in Mayong, Kashyap’s hometown in Assam, and in the tradition of Assamese novelists writing in English.

With the publication of his collection of short stories, His Father’s Disease, in 2019, one noted an expansion, both in terms of the geographical location that extended from Assam to Minnesota and its thematic preoccupation with violence, both personal and political, that stretched to explore issues of identity, sexuality, racism and belonging.

But with his latest novel, Kashyap seems to have shattered barriers of regionalism and set expectations for the writer belonging to the North East, the stranglehold of both of which he had scathingly critiqued in his short story “Skylark Girl,” to write a novel that compels you to place his writing on a wider, even planetary map.

item.title: Trump puts on hold law allowing 100% tariffs on India, four others for buying Russian oil
item.description: The United States president said that waiving the sanctions, which were to take effect on Sunday, was in the interest of the US.
item.content:encoded:
United States President Donald Trump on Friday signed an executive order putting on hold a law that allows him to impose tariffs of up to 100% on India and other countries that purchase Russian oil and gas.

Trump told the US Congress that the waiver was in the interest of the US.

While Trump had given his assent to the legislation on September 18, the signing of the bill into law had not automatically triggered the tariffs.

The law states that the tariffs could apply to the five countries that imported the largest volumes of Russian crude oil or natural gas in the 12 months before the law takes effect, if they knowingly continue buying Russian crude oil 30 days after the law is enacted.

The president’s order pausing the implementation of the law comes before the 30-day period was to conclude on Sunday.

Trump’s decision also came a week after he announced that the US had agreed to purchase diesel from Russia to lower global energy prices. This was despite such a purchase potentially hurting its partner Ukraine in its war with Russia.

Washington has for long claimed that the purchase of Russian energy has been fuelling Moscow’s war on Ukraine, which began in February 2022.

item.title: ‘A line moves people’: Cartoonist Amruta Patil on the graphic narrative exhibition she has curated
item.description: ‘The evolution of graphic storytelling tradition in India is the evolution of our nation,’ she added. ‘A Moving Line’ is on display at MAP, Bengaluru.
item.content:encoded:
Comics have been making their way into museums and art galleries for a while now. Over the last couple of years alone, Kolkata mounted an exhibition on the material craft of comics on the heels of a historical survey of Bengali comics from the 1920s to the present. Delhi’s Kiran Nadar Museum of Art turned itself into an embodied romp across the history of comics, inexplicably buffeted on both sides by a live archive of zines. All this alongside the Comic Cons trudging along each year while the Indie Comix Fests undyingly hop across cities as an open-source, comics-focused alternative.

Cartoonist Amruta Patil’s new exhibition A Moving Line, which opened at MAP Bengaluru on July 24, brings together more than 250 works spanning artefacts across millennia: temple carvings from Bengaluru’s own Someshwara temple to kaavad shrines and pattachitra scrolls; from the Tagore family’s early experiments with social caricature and the Ray family’s patronage for Sandesh to Amar Chitra Katha and Tinkle; from the deflatingly satirical strips of Bengal’s Basantak to glimpses of Pran’s Chacha Chaudhary and Falah Faisal’s Musalman; from thousands of webcomics blooming across platforms to the ongoing boom in graphic novels. It presents, as Patil herself put it, a constellation of idea clusters rather than an exhaustive chronology.

item.title: How the Modi government radicalised a generation to rise in revolt against it
item.description: Ten young protestors in Delhi explain what has angered them and drawn them into the streets.
item.content:encoded:
At around 2 pm on October 2, around one hundred students from the All India Students’ Association made an attempt to reach Jantar Mantar in Delhi. The protestors were demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision of the electoral rolls.

As they approached, they chanted, “Vote Chor, Gaddi Chhod!”, vote thief, leave your seat.

Delhi Police personnel intercepted the group and began to chase protestors in an attempt to detain them. The protestors dodged the police. “Dilli Police wardi kholo, RSS ka knicker pehno!” they chanted as they ran. Delhi police take off your clothes, put on RSS shorts.

item.title: In France, student protests are driven by real concerns but are also a rite of passage
item.description: For many people school demonstrations are a key part of the formation of their role as citizen-protestors.
item.content:encoded:
Across France, school students have taken to the streets to protest about teacher shortages, dilapidated school buildings and long school days.

While the tradition of student protest has long roots in France, the country’s current fiscal crisis combined with entrenched structural problems with teacher recruitment, sickness absence and a backlog of school maintenance means this is unlikely to be something the current government can easily address.

Problems – and protests – regarding conditions in French schools go back decades.

I’ve spent 20 years conducting research in France and protest has been a recurring theme. Many research participants I’ve worked with have spoken with fondness about protesting as high school students.

One participant in Nanterre, who went on to become a community activist, repeatedly spoke about how schools in poor Paris suburbs were institutions that would “crush you”. This was due in part to French educational culture, but also because of their under-resourcing and poor state of repair. To them protest felt like an outlet for these grievances.

item.title: India’s per capita GDP below Bangladesh in 2026: IMF
item.description: The per capita gross domestic product of Bangladesh at current prices is $2,886 against India’s $2,749, the global financial body said.
item.content:encoded:
The International Monetary Fund has said that Bangladesh’s per capita gross domestic product is higher than that of India in 2026.

The per capita gross domestic product of Bangladesh at current prices is $2,886 against India’s $2,749, according to long-term data and forecasts in IMF’s latest World Economic Outlook published on October 13.

Per capita gross domestic product is a measure of a country’s economic output per person. It is calculated by dividing the country's gross domestic product by its population.

The average per capita gross domestic product in emerging markets and developing economies is about $7,746. The global average is about $15,889.

In 2027, Bangladesh’s per capita gross domestic product is estimated to be $3,219, ahead of India’s $3,036, the data showed. Bangladesh will maintain the marginal lead in 2028.

However, in 2029, India’s per capita gross domestic product of $3,661 will top Bangladesh’s $3,334, according to the International Monetary Fund.

A previous version of the report published on April 14 said that the per capita gross domestic product of Bangladesh at current prices at the time was $2,911 against India’s $2,812.

In 2025, India’s per capita gross domestic product was $2,670, marginally ahead of Bangladesh’s $2,635, the data had shown at the time. However, Bangladesh was leading India in 2023 and 2024.

item.title: Peter Nagy (1959-2026): An artist and curator who became a bridge between India and the world
item.description: The American artist-gallerist had an uncanny eye for art across all boundaries – fashion, textiles, ceramics, furniture and even advertising.
item.content:encoded:
Peter Nagy, the artist-gallerist, died on October 13 at the age of at 66.

I knew Peter from my New York days in the late 1980s, before he finally settled in India. He was a fixture in my loft and the parties we had there. He introduced me to many in his circuit, specially the writer Gary Indiana, as much a character of downtown Manhattan as Peter himself.

Peter had studied graphic design and he had started using maps, building plans and similar charts to paint black and white canvases. Mandala patterns and stupa forms became the basis for other works. These evolved into graphic colour images. His work always had an art historic or historic base.

His family had a history of cancer and he showed his cancer series in Delhi last year. He lost the battle against that disease, and after emergency treatment in New York, returned to Delhi to pass away at home with his cats.

item.title: Will the US freeze on green card applications affect Indian IT companies and employees?
item.description: The short-term financial pain may be minimal but there are likely to be long-term effects.

On October 8, the US Department of Labour decided to stop processing PERM labour-certification requests from eight technology firms, including Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL Technologies and Capgemini. The Department of Labor said it would neither accept new applications nor process pending applications involving the named companies.

PERM, or Program Electronic Review Management, is the initial step in the employment-based green-card process for most immigrants applying under the EB-2 and EB-3 categories. In order to proceed to the next stage, employers are required to prove that they have tried to hire Americans for the jobs in question.

The processing of the applications has been suspended in accordance with 20 CFR § 656.31(b), which allows for the temporary interruption of services if there are grounds to believe that fraud or wilful misrepresentation is involved.

A fresh coat of white paint failed to obscure the old cracks on the office walls where the ambassador sat behind his desk in all his fleshy bulk, his rough, ungainly hands wiping the sweat from his face with whatever was closest: a corner of his jacket, the report on our prospects for the oil deal, the photograph of his only daughter. Behind him, the map of India nailed to the wall still owned to a vestigial East Pakistan, and next to this, portraits of Gandhi, Indira, Nehru and Rao hung like long-forgotten family members.

They were sending me to San Francisco, to the consulate there, though why, he didn’t know, and saying that he laughed, a real crack-up of a laugh. item.title: As the Pope recovers from lung cancer surgery, disease risk among non-smokers is growing
item.description: Identifying potential causes such as environmental exposures and genetics are a challenge when it comes to screening more people.
item.content:encoded:
When many people think of an average lung cancer patient, they often imagine an older man smoking. But the face of lung cancer has changed. Over the past 15 years, more women, never smokers and younger people are being diagnosed with lung cancer.

In fact, lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death among women, and more women die from lung cancer than breast, ovarian and colorectal cancer each year. The American Lung Association reports that while lung cancer rates have risen by 79% for women over the last 44 years, they decreased by 43% for men. And for the first time in history, there are more young women than men diagnosed with lung cancer.

News about Pope Leo XIV’s lung cancer diagnosis on Oct. 13, 2026, sparked discussion about increasing rates of the disease among people who have never smoked. Leo reportedly is not a smoker. Potential causes for the disease include environmental exposures and genetics, and recognising the diverse factors that can increase someone’s risk of lung cancer – regardless of their smoking history – is essential for timely and appropriate screening and treatment.

item.description: An excerpt from ‘I Was the Wind Last Night: New and Selected Poems’, by Ruskin Bond.
item.content:encoded:
Cherry Tree

Eight years have passed
Since I placed my cherry seed in the grass.
“Must have a tree of my own,” I said—
And watered it once and went to bed
And forgot; but cherries have a way of growing
Though no one’s caring very much or knowing,
And suddenly that summer, near the end of May,
I found a tree had come to stay.
It was very small, a five months’ child,
Lost in the tall grass running wild.
Goats ate the leaves, a grasscutter’s scythe
Split it apart, and a monsoon blight
Shrivelled the slender stem… Even so,
Next spring I watched three new shoots grow,
The young tree struggle, upwards thrust
Its arms in a fresh fierce lust
For light and air and sun.

Who watches, wondering, while

“Restrained, detained, contained,” said the front page banner headline of the newspaper, describing the events of the previous day.

The jeweller grumbled and put it more pithily: “Such a nuisance.”

On Saturday, thousands of ordinary citizens had defied the unprecedented security cover in Central Delhi to show up to protest against the chief election commissioner who they believe is rigging voter lists in the ruling party’s favour.

To thwart the protest, the government had cancelled trains, closed down metro stations, and even shuttered markets like Karol Bagh.

item.title: Becoming Agarwal: A new book examines how a dominant mercantile caste sustains its privilege today
item.description: An excerpt from the Introduction to ‘Becoming Agarwal: The Manufacture of a Close-Knit Mercantile Caste’, by Ujithra Ponniah.

The “new” Hindu India is an elite, exclusionary and violent project characterised by an ethnic democracy led by members of wealthy “upper”-caste Hindu groups and increasingly finding cultural resonance across caste groups. An ethnic democracy is one in which there is a two-tiered citizenship, with the majority having more rights than the minority. The BJP is traditionally seen as the Brahmin-Bania party. The majority rise of the BJP in 2014 and again for a second term in 2019 has seen an increase in the structural power of business.

In 2009, [Christophe] Jaffrelot and [Narender] Kumar wrote about the “plebeianisation” – or the rise of the lower castes in political power – by showing how the share of upper-caste members of legislative assemblies (MLAs) has steadily declined in many states from the 1950s to the 2000s. item.title: The pure feast of colour that is Kamal Amrohi’s ‘Pakeezah’
item.description: The interweave of emotion and colour stands out in a restoration carried out by Film Heritage Foundation along with Kamal Amrohi’s family.
item.content:encoded:
In Kamal Amrohi’s Pakeezah, there are early references to colour and the psychological states it evokes.

The courtesan Nargis tells her aristocratic lover Shahabuddin who has promised to marry her that she can already imagine the house they will be living in. The house will be white, like their pure love. Nargis dreams of crossing the threshold dressed in bridal red threads.

As the story unfolds, viewers learn that Nargis’s profession comes in the way of the marriage, leading to her early death. Shahabuddin switches to black sherwanis, the shade of mourning as he hunts for Sahebjaan, the daughter he has had with Nargis.

Sahebjaan is the leading light of Delhi’s pleasure quarter. Bedecked out in an array of bright ensembles (flame orange, coral pink, emerald green), Sahebjaan entices her patrons even as she longs to be known as “pakeezah”, the symbol of purity and respectability. Away from the dance floor, Sahebjaan is seen mostly in white, the colour-coded expression of her yearning.

The Indian government and Life Insurance Corporation will sell 60.7% stake in IDBI Bank for Rs 52,878 crore to Canadian financial holding company Fairfax Financial Holdings Limited, said the Union Ministry of Finance on Wednesday.

The divestment would bring the “largest foreign direct investment in the financial sector of our economy so far”, added the ministry.

It said that IDBI Bank had “required repeated infusion of capital, initially provided by the Government of India” and later by Life Insurance Corporation.

In view of this, the Reserve Bank of India imposed several restrictions on the bank and the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs approved strategic restructuring of the financial institution.

“In compliance thereof, it was decided that an aggregate 60.72% of the equity stake in the IDBI Bank Limited be sold to a strategic buyer,” said the ministry. This would leave a shareholding of 15% with the Union government and 19% with Life Insurance Corporation.

My favourite newspaper no longer exists. It was called the Bombay Chronicle, and it was founded in 1910 as a nationalist alternative to the British-owned and British-oriented Times of India. In the first half of the 20th century, Bombay was an incredibly exciting place to live and work in. It was British India’s commercial capital, and also the epicentre of the film industry, of nationalist politics, and of much else besides. The excitement and intensity of the times was vividly captured in the pages of the Bombay Chronicle. The newspaper had many fine reporters and two outstanding editors: BG Horniman, who was at the helm in its early years, and SA Brelvi, who edited it in the 1920s and 1930s.

item.title: What is the most serious threat we face today? This book argues it is accelerating climate change
item.description: An excerpt from ‘Life in the Time of Polycrisis’, by G Madhusoodanan.
item.content:encoded:
The severest manifestation of the global polycrisis is climate change. The Earth’s climate is regulated by an enormously complex melange of interrelated processes, forming part of the planetary ecological web. The web includes the sun, the atmosphere, the lithosphere, the hydrosphere, the cryosphere, and the biosphere. These are interrelated and interact through many natural cycles or biogeochemical cycles. Scientific understanding of the Earth’s climate system progressed significantly in the twentieth century. The pioneer of climate science, the late Wallace Broecker, warned in 1987 that interfering in natural systems not fully scientifically understood is like “playing Russian roulette which may result in unpleasant surprises”, because no one knows what lies in the active chamber of the gun.

Russian roulette players know the risky game they are playing. But humans hardly knew the consequences when they embarked on the path of modern fossil-fuel-powered economic growth.

However, at the beginning of 1980, when empirical evidence emerged about the impact on climate, the initial reaction of governments and corporations was denial, and the denial industry continues even today. We are now in a climate emergency which is set within the larger interconnected polycrisis.

item.title: By rewriting textbooks, India is weakening spirit of enquiry mandated by the Constitution
item.description: As Indian students are forced to view medieval history through a polarised lens, the country’s democratic fabric faces a deep philosophical crisis.
item.content:encoded:
The new social science textbook for Class 9 students released by the National Council of Educational Research and Training has removed chapters on European revolutions to prioritise medieval Indian history through the lens of “Resistance and Resilience” against successive foreign invasions.

The textbook. titled Understanding Society: India and Beyond (Part 2), argues that the Indian subcontinent faced successive phases of invasions driven by territorial expansion and religious motives. It details the brutality of the Mughal state against Sikh gurus, alongside regional uprisings such as the Jat Uprising of 1669 against heavy agrarian taxation and religious policies.

While these historical conflicts and state oppressions are matters of historical record that deserve rigorous study, framing the entire medieval past through a monolithic, black-and-white binary of Muslim invasion versus Hindu resistance flattens the complex, messy realities of history. It replaces nuanced historical analysis with a political narrative of perpetual civilisational grievance.

By reducing history to an unceasing clash of religious forces, such textbooks commit a grave erase the profound cultural osmosis that occurred simultaneously at the grassroots level. History is rarely just a process of state-on-state violence or imperial conquest. A dominant strain of Indian strategic thought is anchored in a sense of civilisational greatness, powered by a collective memory of colonial subjugation, racism and systemic exclusion. This narrative overlaps several political timelines. During the freedom struggle, it was about emerging from colonial rule as a great power. But for the Hindu nationalists, it was also about shedding the shame of all past invasions into India, particularly by Muslim Mughals, and about Hindu pride. During the Cold War, it was about economic and political discrimination and nuclear “apartheid”, among others. In the post-Cold War world, it was about non-interference, US sanctions and the ills of American unipolarity.

For much of its post-Independence history, Indian behaviour expressed a siege mindset, born of persistent strategic anxieties that left its leaders little room to effectively articulate the country’s rightful place in the world. This sense of vulnerability and insecurity was a constant in the Indian strategic imagination. The sense of anxiety in the Indian political culture was felt across party divides. However, since the turn of the millennium, the “postcolonial insignificance” and external‘disciplinary pressures’ that once constrained New Delhi have dramatically diminished. item.title: ‘The Loves of a Mogul Prince’: The forgotten film that first tapped into the Anarkali legend
item.description: The movie would have been the first adaptation of the famous Imtiaz Ali Taj play ‘Anarkali’.
item.content:encoded:
In Indian popular culture, Salim and Anarkali are firmly embedded as being among the greatest lovers of all time. While the historical veracity of their forbidden romance – or whether Anarkali existed at all – is disputed, there is no debate about the role played by cinema in immortalising the legend.

Several screen versions of the story, most of them drawing heavily from the famous Imtiaz Ali Taj play Anarkali, have captivated audiences for nearly a century now. There is Nandlal Jaswantlal’s Anarkali (1953), starring Pradeep Kumar and Bina Rai and featuring a fabulous soundtrack by C Ramchandra. There is K Asif’s all-time classic Mughal-e-Azam (1960), starring Prithviraj Kapoor, Dilip Kumar and Madhubala.

Before these films, there was the Imperial Film Company’s silent movie Anarkali in 1928, which made Sulochana an even bigger star, and its talkie remake in 1935. Were it not for the acumen of Imperial Film Company founder Ardeshir Irani, another film titled The Loves of A Mogul Prince would have been the first adaptation of the doomed romance.

Adani Group’s flagship firm began the 2022 financial year in a slump but ended it with a 200% jump in profits. Over 70% of the annual turnover of the firm, Adani Enterprises Limited, came from its coal import division. “The business witnessed an astronomical rise in the volumes pertaining to the supplies made to various state or central owned electricity generation companies,” the firm said in its annual report for 2022-’23.

In May 2022, citing domestic coal shortages, India’s power ministry had directed all thermal power producing companies in the country to mandatorily import 10% of their coal needs.

The import mandate coincided with a surge in international coal prices. item.title: Why relocating wild animals is rife with complications
item.description: The social dimensions of moving wildlife were considered much less consistently than biological ones
item.content:encoded:
Moving large animals around is a seductive idea in conservation. If there are plenty of animals in one place and too few in another, moving some between the two seems an obvious solution. Sometimes it is. But with animals as large, mobile and socially complicated as elephants and rhinos, the move itself can turn out to be the straightforward part.

This autumn, 12 rhinos are due to be moved from a well-established reserve in North West Province in South Africa to another protected area, in the Waterberg region, as part of efforts to establish and strengthen secure rhino populations. I am involved with the conservation work around the move, including research that will follow what happens after the rhinos arrive.

But there are lessons from past projects that we have to bear in mind. In 2022, 263 elephants were moved around 350km from Liwonde National Park in Malawi to another park in Malawi, Kasungu National Park. Decades of poaching had severely depleted Kasungu’s elephants, while successful protection in Liwonde had allowed its population to grow. With Malawi’s protected areas increasingly isolated from one another, moving elephants from a relatively dense population to a much larger park with relatively few elephants made good sense.

item.title: Why Anne Carson has won the Nobel Prize for Literature: For her bold, inventive, breathtaking work
item.description: The distance between classical literature and contemporary life shrinks thoroughly and repeatedly across her work.
item.content:encoded:
Anne Carson has been awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature. The 76-year-old Canadian poet, essayist, translator and classicist was in Iceland “listening to the wind” when the news broke. The Swedish Academy praised her “bold and inventive” oeuvre for its “playful dialogue with the classical tradition”, through which she has fashioned “new forms for contemporary literature”.

In books like her 1998 verse novel Autobiography of Red (which has sold nearly 100,000 copies in the United States), Wrong Norma (2024), her recent poetry collection, and her 1986 debut Eros the Bittersweet – a book-length essay about the god of love – she challenges formal conventions and moves across literary genres.

Carson’s own account of what language can do offers a sense of the possibilities such invention opens up:

“words can squirt sideways, mute and mad; you think they are tools, or toys, or tame, and all at once they burn all your clothes off and you’re standing there singed and ridiculous in the glare of the lightning.'“

‘The easiest difficult poet’

Born in Toronto in 1950, Carson studied classics at the University of Toronto and went on to teach ancient Greek. Eros the Bittersweet grew out of her scholarly training.

item.title: The economy is made of people: Lessons from the Economics Nobel for India
item.description: Macroeconomic outcomes cannot be fully understood without examining the individual decisions that produce them.
item.content:encoded:
What does a central bank’s interest-rate decision mean to a household struggling with food prices, a small business deciding whether to expand or a company weighing a new investment? These may seem like very different questions. Yet they lie at the heart of a single economic problem: how do the decisions of households and businesses shape the wider economy and how can public policy influence those decisions?

This question sits at the centre of the work recognised by the 2026 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences, awarded to Robert E Hall of Stanford University and Michael Woodford of Columbia University “for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation”. Their research helps explain why understanding an economy requires looking beyond aggregate indicators to the choices, expectations and constraints of the people and firms that make it function.

For India, this is more than a theoretical insight. The latest figures show retail inflation rising to 5.54% in September from 4.83% in August, while food inflation climbed to 7.74%. The burden is not evenly distributed: rural headline inflation reached 6.08%, compared with 4.88% in urban areas.

“China has never recognised the so-called Union Territory of Ladakh unilaterally and illegally established by India,” the state-owned media portal quoted Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning as saying.

Responding to this, India’s Ministry of External Affairs stated that Ladakh “is an integral and inalienable part of India”.

“No amount of denial by the Chinese side can change this established fact,” said the ministry.

On October 2, India identified 28 places, including several sites in Aksai Chin, on the official Indian map. China occupies the Aksai Chin, which India states is part of its Union Territory of Ladakh.

item.content:encoded:
The 0.4% fee on Unified Payments Interface transactions above Rs 2,000 to merchants will be imposed after the Hindu festival of Diwali, which will be celebrated on November 8 this year, said the National Payments Corporation of India on Tuesday.

The corporation is an umbrella body of retail payments and settlement systems operating under the Reserve Bank of India.

On September 14 and September 15, the Ministry of Finance issued notifications stating that UPI payments to merchants valued above Rs 2,000 would attract a merchant discount rate of 0.4%.

A merchant discount rate is a fee charged to businesses by banks to cover the costs of processing transactions. The rate typically ranges from 1% to 3% of the transaction value for credit card payments and can be up to 0.9% for debit card transactions.

On September 28, the Union government said that the charges would take effect on October 15.

The National Payments Corporation of India said on Tuesday that the decision to defer the implementation of the charges was taken “keeping in mind the festive season”.
